Good morning, everyone. I call to order the seventh informal meeting of the plenary on the question of equitable representation on an increase in the membership of the Security Council and other matters related to the Council. My fellow co-chair and I would like to extend a very warm welcome to all of you. And we would like to thank all delegations for their active and constructive participation during the IGM plenary on April 14th.

As indicated in our letter dated 7 April, at this morning's meeting, we will invite the delegation of Sierra Leone in its capacity as coordinator of the African Union Committee of 10 on United Nations Security Council reform to present the African model. Delegations were invited to inscribe on the list of speakers via e-delegate, and the live link to the list of speakers was circulated to all delegations. At this stage, any delegation who wishes to be added to the existing list of speakers should inform the Secretariat table. Any delegation wishing to speak on behalf of a group of states should inform the Secretariat in order to be given priority. We also encourage delegations to adhere to the time limits we have established. Statements delivered on behalf of a group of states will be limited to five minutes, and national statements will be limited to three minutes. To assist speakers with time management, we have projected the on-screen timer on the screens. We encourage delegations to listen to each other, engage constructively, and seek areas of convergence in our meetings. In that light, we invite delegations to focus their intervention on any evolution in their positions, including new elements they may wish to highlight. Once the list of speakers is exhausted, we will hold an interactive discussion on the African model and allow for member states and groups of states to respond to views and proposals put forth in a closed meeting without webcast.

And before we begin, I would like to remind members that delegations are encouraged to e-mail a copy of their statements to e-statements@un.org for the publication on the repository website, as well as to facilitate interpretation. We will first hear the presentation of the model submitted by Sierra Leone in its capacity as coordinator of the African Union Committee of 10, C10, on United Nations Security Council reform. And I welcome the distinguished representative of Sierra Leone, who is represented here at the podium together with us. And I now invite the distinguished representative of Sierra Leone to proceed with the presentation of the African model. You have the floor.

Thank you very much, Madam Distinguished Co-Chair. Distinguished Co-Chairs, Excellencies, distinguished delegates. I have the honor on behalf of the African member states to introduce the African reform model on United Nations Security Council reform, endorsed at the 39th ordinary session of the Assembly of Heads of State and Government of the African Union, held from 14 to 15 February 2026 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia. I sincerely thank you, distinguished co-chairs, for convening this structured dialogue and for your continued efforts to advance this important Member States-driven process through these dialogues. Africa values the intergovernmental negotiations as the appropriate platform for open, transparent, and substantive engagement on Security Council reform. We also welcome the effort to move this process from general reaffirmations to a more focused engagement on reform models. This is necessary. Indeed, it is long overdue, given the urgency of the reform. Excellencies, the imperative for Security Council reform is no longer in doubt. What remains in question is whether the process is prepared to confront with seriousness and consequence the central injustice at the heart of the current structure of the Council, the continued exclusion and underrepresentation of Africa. This injustice is historical, it is structural, and it is indefensible. Africa was not adequately at the table in 1945 when the Charter was negotiated and when the architecture of the Security Council was established. Most African countries were still under colonial domination and therefore had no voice in shaping the post-war multilateral order. Yet, the United Nations is currently comprised of 54 African member states, making it the largest regional grouping in the organization, and African issues dominate the Security Council's agenda. Africa has not been a mere recipient of the UN support, but an active contributor to its success, and is therefore a key actor for the maintenance of international peace and security. Africa is central to peacekeeping, peacebuilding, mediation, and post-conflict recovery. And still, Africa remains without representation in the permanent category of the Security Council. This reality cannot be justified politically, legally, morally, and it cannot be sustained institutionally. This is why Africa has consistently maintained that any credible reform of the Security Council must, as a matter of priority, redress the historical injustice against Africa and treat Africa as a special case. This is the minimum condition for legitimacy as agreed in the Pact for the Future. As was convincingly captured during the historic Security Council high-level debate on addressing the historical injustice and enhancing Africa's effective representation on the UN Security Council in August 2024, held during Sierra Leone's presidency of the Council, Africa remains permanently on the menu of the Security Council, but not permanently at the table. This distills with clarity the lived contradiction of the present order, a continent that is constantly the subject of deliberation, yet systematically denied equal authority in decision making. This contradiction must end. The formulation that Africa is, and I quote, "permanently on the menu," end of quote, but does not have a permanent seat at the table captures the deeper historical truth underpinning Africa's claim that the continent has endured a long arc of exclusion from slavery and colonialism, the Berlin partition, to the construction of a post-1945 order in which Africa was acted upon more often than it was permitted to act. The injustice, therefore, is not abstract. It is historical, structural, and ongoing. To be clear, the problem is not that the case for Africa has not been made. The case has been made repeatedly, consistently, and convincingly over decades. The problem is that some have too often preferred acknowledgement over action, sympathy over structural correction, and procedural comfort over political courage. Africa comes to this process united and prepared with a clear, coherent, and fully articulated common position for over two decades. The African model now before the membership is not a new position. It is the structured and detailed presentation of the common African position as contained in the Azuwini Consensus and the State Declaration, and further reflected in the 2015 framework document inputs of the African group and reflection of relevant language from Action 39A of the Pact for the Future to treat Africa as a special case and priority in the reform process. Distinguished Co-Chairs, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, let me now briefly present Africa's position across the five IGN clusters, as well as the question of treating Africa as a special case and priority. On categories of membership, Africa's position is clear. Reform limited to the non-permanent category is no reform at all in addressing the historical injustice against Africa and the current structural imbalance in the Council. Africa calls for an enlarged Security Council of no fewer than 26 seats. Within the reform Council, the permanent category should total 11 seats including no fewer than two permanent seats for Africa. The non-permanent category should total no fewer than 15 seats, including five non-permanent seats for Africa. The African Union will select Africa's representative for submission to the General Assembly for election. The two permanent seats and five non-permanent seats for Africa is the minimum required to begin correcting the present injustice. The Assembly must also recognize that Article 23 of the Charter defines only two categories of membership. Proposals that seek to create intermediate, longer-term, or other transitional categories as a substitute for permanent seats for Africa do not resolve the problem, nor do they align with the UN Charter. They merely preserve the inequality in another form. Africa, therefore, reiterates that equitable reform must address both existing categories of membership, not invent alternatives that dilute the question of justice. On regional representation, Africa's position is equally clear and firm. Any reform that seeks to ensure fair and equitable geographical representation in the Security Council must reflect the principles, objectives, and ideals of the Charter including universalism, equity, and regional balance. The current composition of the Council does not accurately reflect the diversity of the United Nations membership, particularly in relation to Africa, which has long been underrepresented in the non-permanent category and excluded from the permanent category. Africa is one of the largest regions in terms of membership, population, and political weight in the multilateral system. The African Union and its member states play an increasingly important role in the maintenance of international peace and security. The African voice is therefore not peripheral to the work of the Council, it is central to it. A Council that continues to marginalize Africa cannot command the legitimacy required for the discharge of its primary responsibility under the Charter. On the size of an enlarged Security Council and working method, Africa strongly support an enlarged Council of at least 26 seats in order to reflect contemporary geopolitical realities and to ensure more representative participation. Africa also maintains that reform cannot be reduced to the question of seats alone. A more representative Council must also be more accessible, more democratic, and more transparent, more accountable, and more responsive to the broader membership. Working methods matter, and significant work continues to be done to improve the working methods, including on equal access to Council documents, an issue advanced by Algeria during its 2024-2025 tenure on the Council, securing the inclusion of new provisions in Note 507 that affirm that all members of the Council shall be afforded the same level of access to documentation. Working methods remain integral to comprehensive reform. But let there be no misunderstanding. Improvement in working methods cannot be offered as a substitute for reform in categories of membership. Processes cannot replace justice. The African model and the 2015 framework document clearly sets out Africa's expectation in this regard. On the question of the veto, Africa's position is longstanding and unambiguous. Africa remains opposed to the veto in principle. However, so long as the veto continues to exist, it cannot remain the exclusive reserve of a few. If it is retained, it must be extended to all permanent members, including the new permanent seats allocated to Africa. There can be no reform that creates a permanent new permanent members, but denies them the right and prerogatives attached to permanent membership. That will not be reform. That will be discrimination by a design. Africa will not accept equality in name and inequality in substance. Now, does Africa see any benefit in postponing discussions of the veto until after agreement on the composition of the council? The veto is interconnected with the other clusters including categories of membership, regional representation, size, and working methods. A genuine reform must therefore address these questions squarely and honestly. On the relationship between the Security Council and the General Assembly, Africa affirms the need for a more amonious, cooperative, and constitutionally balanced relationship between the two principal organs. Both must work closely within their respective mandate under the Charter to address the many challenges facing the international community. Africa supports a relationship that strengthens complementarity, enhances accountability, and preserves the institutional balance intended by the Charter. On this cluster, Africa's position is clearly reflected in the 2015 framework document and the reform model. Distinguished co-chairs, in addition to the five clusters, Africa continues to stress one fundamental political requirement. Africa must be treated as a special case and priority in the reform process. This is not an extraneous issue. It is central to the logic of reform itself. The Pact for the Future has reinforced what Africa has been emphasizing for decades, that the historical injustice against Africa must be addressed as a matter of priority. that must be now translated from declarative language into an operative outcome. Overall, Africa's position is therefore both principled and practical. It is principled because it is rooted in justice, equity, and historical correction. It is practical because it places before this process a clear and comprehensive model across all five clusters. The time has come for the IG to move beyond rhetorical sympathy and towards serious engagement with Africa's proposal. This must be manifested in the consolidated model our leaders agreed to be developed, a model that must take fully into account the common African position in order to be able to move this reform process one step forward in this session. On engaging in tax-based negotiation, we state our position that Africa is only to engage in tax-based negotiation provided there is a prior consensus between member states on the five clusters and a grid framework which broadly addresses the issue of historical injustice that has wide consensus and a model of reform that clearly addresses expansion in both categories of the Security Council. In closing, distinguished co-chairs, excellencies, distinguished delegates, the current structure of the United Nations Security Council reflect a bygone era and does not adequately recognize Africa's important role and the maintenance of international peace and security, including the continent's substantial contributions to peacekeeping and peace support operations. With a population of over 1.4 billion people, Africa remains insufficiently represented in the principal structures of global decision-making, particularly in the Security Council. The African model calls for urgent and meaningful reform to ensure a council that is more inclusive, more representative and more responsive to contemporary global realities. Therefore, welcome your thoughts and question. I thank you.

I thank His Excellency, the distinguished representative of Sierra Leone for his comprehensive briefing. A large part of the puzzle at hand has been put in place. A more comprehensive picture of the way forward is at hand. I now open the floor for discussions and comments on the presentation. Germany, please, you have the floor.

Distinguished Co-Chairs, thank you for your work and thank you for giving me the floor. I have the honor to speak on behalf of the G4, Brazil, India, Japan, and my own country, Germany.

And let me first of all.

Thank our colleague, the ambassador from Sierra Leone, for his briefing on the African model this morning. For decades, the IGN has not made any real progress, but now we have reached an important point. Three years ago, the IGM agreed to move towards concrete discussions of reform models, and today we have crossed an important threshold. Now that the African group has presented its reform model, we can move on to take the next step together. We now have before us all the essential elements to develop a consolidated model as agreed by all in the Pact for the Future on the basis of models presented by member states thus far. As the G4, we fully support the African model. We share the same objective, a meaningful reform of the Council that reflects today's geopolitical realities. We share the same vision for Council reform, which must include an expansion of membership in both the permanent and the non-permanent categories. Both models address the urgent need to redress the historical injustice against Africa and improve the representation of the underrepresented and unrepresented regions in the Security Council. We also note that Africa's model envisioning a Council of "not less than 26 members" is compatible with the G4's model. The African and G4 proposals of enhancing transparency and participation in the work of the Council are converging as well. Even on the issue of veto, our position and that of our African group are also aligned in that new permanent members should, as a principle, have the same responsibilities and obligations as current ones. This alignment is politically very significant. It is a powerful confirmation of the broad convergence that exists among many member states. A clear majority supports expansion in both categories, not only Africa and the G4, but also L69, CARICOM, the Arab Group, Benelux and the Nordics. The direction of the membership is clear and their desire is real. For this very reason, this convergence must now be translated into concrete progress. We cannot continue to circle around established positions forever without trying to achieve progress. The time has come to develop without further delay, a consolidated model on the basis of Member States' proposals that have been presented in the IGN. The consolidated model must faithfully reflect the very strong support for enlargement in both categories, including the rightful representation of Africa, alongside other unrepresented and underrepresented regions in the permanent category. This must be a precursor to text-based negotiations. I thank you very much.
I thank the distinguished representative of Germany, and I give the floor to Italy.

Thank you, distinguished co-chairs. I make this intervention on behalf of Uniting for Consensus, a pro-reform, cross-regional, and diversified group composed by Argentina, Canada, Colombia, Costa Rica, Italy, Malta, Mexico, Pakistan, Republic of Korea, San Marino, Spain, and Turkey. I wish to thank Sierra Leone for presenting the model for reform of the Security Council on behalf of the C10 African Group. It is a valuable effort to address the long-standing issues surrounding the Council's composition and functioning. The African Group has demonstrated the clear leadership in the process. It was the first negotiating group to articulate a unified position through the adoption of the Sirta Declaration and the Ezulwini Consensus, and most recently, through the submission of its reform model. By putting forward this proposal, Africa has contributed towards shaping a common understanding of a comprehensive reform. UFC, like the African model, supports the call for more equitable and balanced representation of Africa and other underrepresented regions in the Council. This would not only remedy the current geographical imbalance, but also benefit us all by making the reformed Council truly representative to the wider membership. It will be key to implement this common goal without reproducing existing inequalities, but rather ensuring that the Council becomes more representative, democratic, accountable, transparent and effective. In 2024, world leaders recognized the need as a priority to address the historical injustice against Africa, recognizing it as a special case, while also improving the representation of the underrepresented and unrepresented regions and groups, such as Asia Pacific and Latin America and the Caribbean.

We

support this approach and acknowledge the importance that African countries attach to ensuring the voice of their region is fully

heard.

UFC sympathizes with Africa, whose proposal has been framed as a collective regional effort, fundamentally different from the one driven by individual national ambitions. UFC's position on the expansion of the permanent category and its prerogatives is well known, and we believe that our model has built-in flexibility to adequately accommodate African aspirations in a constructive and forward-looking manner. UFC wishes to engage more closely with Africa to share and understand each other's perspectives and to pursue our common objectives. UFC concurs with the African model on several issues, including the need to improve working methods. We share the view that enlargement alone is insufficient, as any reform must address the Council's effectiveness. Enhancing transparency must remain central. This is why we also support a more inclusive decision-making. Closer cooperation between the Council and the Peacebuilding Commission and the African Union's Peace and Security Council is a priority. Aligned with the Peacebuilding Commission and African Union priorities, equitable decision-making and genuine localization are essential, not just in principle, but in practice. to ensure more effective and sustainable delivery on the ground. Another element of convergence between the two models is the relationship between the Security Council and the General Assembly. UFC, as well as Africa, has always called for a reform that would strengthen coordination and complementarity between the two organs and guarantee greater accountability. Likewise, we both advocate for greater inclusions of non-council members in the discussions of issues that directly affect them. We would welcome your reflections on the concept of cross-regional representation, especially concerning the possible establishment of cross-regional seats. We would also be interested in understanding how the African model envisions ensuring accountability and periodic review of members that would hypothetically hold permanent seats, given that such a status would not be subject to election. Finally, we would like to request your assessment on the impact of a reduced ratio of elective to permanent members in terms of preserving the democratic character of its decision making. In the spirit of mutual flexibility, we look forward to building on convergences with the African group and other negotiating groups and member states to reach an agreement on a proposal that enjoys the widest possible political acceptance. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Italy. I give the floor to Sweden.

Colleagues, I have the honor to speak on behalf of the Nordic countries, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, and my own country, Sweden. Let me begin by expressing our gratitude to you, Ambassador Albanai and Ambassador Gregoire van Haren, for continued efforts as co-chairs of the IGM process. In the Pact for the Future, our leaders decided to encourage the submission of further models with a view to developing a consolidated model in the future. It is now time to deliver on this commitment and support your steadfast leadership towards presenting a consolidated model. We thank the representative of Sierra Leone for the presentation and welcome the submission of the African Union Member States model, and we also thank the African Union Committee for their work. Co-Chairs, equitable representation is an essential part of reform. And we have all agreed to view Africa as a special case. The Nordics support a geographically balanced expansion of the Council. And as part of redressing the historical injustice done to the African continent, we support seats for Africa in both categories of Security Council membership. The Nordic countries have read the African model with great interest and will study it further. We welcome its clear objectives and added detail. With your permission, co-chairs, we have selected a few questions. On categories of membership and regional representation. On the no less than two new permanent seats for Africa to be selected by the African Union, What type of appointments do you foresee to specific countries on fixed seats or rotating regional representation for these two seats? How would the five African non-permanent seats relate to cross-regional representation, both within the regions of Africa and more broadly, including, for example, SIDS or Arab states in Africa? Co-Chairs, on the size of an enlarged Security Council, it is important that an expansion does not negatively impact the full participation of all Council members. We note with interest the proposals under section C, aiming at, among other things, strengthening the Council's collaboration with troop contributing countries and increasing transparency and access to documentation. However, we believe that a decision to expand the Council to a total of not less than 26 members also needs concrete changes to the Council's day-to-day working methods to ensure full participation of all members, including changes in Note 507. Do you foresee to propose any such additional changes? We also welcome the reference to the work of the subsidiary organs. Any thoughts or views on how an enlarged Council could avoid the type of impasse that we currently see regarding allocations of chairmanships? The proposed model seems to suggest that the Council cannot engage on any issue that does not constitute a threat to international peace and security. How does this correspond to the thematic work of the Council and to the Council's authority under Chapter VI? Co-Chairs, The Nordic countries welcome the importance that the African model attaches to the role and authority of the General Assembly in the context of Security Council reform, and we note with interest the priorities listed under section E. The Nordic countries support greater transparency and interaction between the Security Council and the General Assembly, as well as the General Assembly fulfilling its own role on matters of international peace and security, particularly when the Council is unable to act. Finally, the Nordic countries believe that any reform should include a review clause, not as a means to make temporary arrangements, but as to set a moment with a fixed deadline to assess our reforms and make further adjustments as necessary. We would like to ask if a review clause has been considered. Co-chairs, colleagues, the time for reform is now. More than ever, the world needs a Security Council that is better equipped, more representative, more effective. But it is only by bridging our differences with determination and a spirit of compromise that we will be able to deliver meaningful reform. The Nordic countries look forward to continuing this important work together with you. Thank you, Mr. Chair.

I thank the distinguished representative of Sweden.

And I give the floor to the Kingdom of Bahrain.

At the outset, I

wish to express our thanks to the permanent representative of Kuwait, Mr. Tarek Al-Bunay. and the Permanent Representative of the Netherlands, we congratulate you for your stewardship of our work, and we thank you for your efforts to safeguard this important negotiating process. The Arab Group affirms that The presentation of comprehensive models like the African model are steps in the right direction to move from discussions to more precise and realistic approaches to bring together the points of view between states. We welcome the efforts carried out by the C-10 and the African Union to present a unified African position based on consensus like the Cirt Declaration and the Ezewtini Consensus, reflecting a clear vision seeking to correct historic imbalances with regards to the representation of the African continent on the Security Council. Our group takes note of the fact that this model includes advanced elements with regard to dealing with issues such as the category of member and the veto and regional groups. And this model seeks to devote two, at least two permanent seats to Africa, as well as five non-permanent seats, underscoring the principle of equality in law and privileges and rights. and on the veto if this is to be retained and the idea is to ensure more equity in representation on the Council. Now the Arab group, while taking note of this position, believes that any reform model must be based on an essential principle, which is correcting the imbalances in terms of geographic representation and ensuring that the Security Council reflects contemporary international reality. in particular when it comes to underrepresented areas, including the Arab group. So in this context, the Arab group underscores that any expansion of the category of a permanent member must include permanent Arab representation with all necessary privileges in order to reflect the political and demographic weight of our group. We also believe that any expansion in the category of non-permanent seats must take account of the need to ensure that the Arab group is represented in a balanced manner in an expanded council. With regard to the veto, we believe that the position of the African group, which calls for it to be repealed or, if it is to continue, for it to be extended to all permanent members, reflects a principle based on justice and equality. That is a principle that must govern any reform approach. We also underscore that discussions on the veto must be coupled with efforts seeking to strengthen transparency and accountability for its use, for the use of the veto to guarantee more credibility for the Council. With regard to regional representation, now the Arab group underscores the need to recognize its unique characteristics as a political group, as a fully fledged political group, so that Arab representation isn't watered down by a more broader regional group, and this is to guarantee a just balance that reflects the political and geographic realities of the Arab group. We also underscored that the models put forward, in particular the African model, show how important it is to adopt a comprehensive approach that deals with the category of members, regional representation, and the working methods of the Council and relationship with the General Assembly in order to guarantee a comprehensive and not partial reform. By way of conclusion, we reiterate that Security Council reform must be a comprehensive process that is based between balance between justice, representation, and efficacy. Any reform model must contribute to strengthening the capacity of the Council to discharge its role the maintenance of international peace and security, as reflected in the Charter, and we are committed to working constructively in order to reach an understanding that will lead us to a true reform. To conclude, I thank you for your relentless efforts in this process, and I thank the representative of Sierra Leone for presenting the African model. Thank you.
And I give the floor to Saint Lucia.

Thank you, co-chairs. And on behalf of the L69 group, we continue to thank the coaches for their leadership in this process. Today, I have the honor to speak on behalf of the L69 group, and our group takes the opportunity to welcome with genuine appreciation the formal submission of the African model as presented by Ambassador Michael Kanu of Sierra Leone in his capacity as C10 coordinator. We commend the C10 for the clarity and the conviction with which the with which Africa has articulated its position and for the leadership Africa has consistently demonstrated throughout this long and unfinished reform process the l69 group and the C10 do not merely share positions the founding document of this group A/61/L69/Rev.1 was guided from the outset by the same recognition that undergirds the African model, that the Security Council cannot credibly discharge its mandates so as long as the regions most affected by its decisions remain most excluded from its deliberations. The L69 and the C10, constituted by developing countries, are, in this respect, strikingly similar. The L69 group reaffirms unequivocally its full support for the common African position. We recognize and support consistently with our long-standing practice that Africa must have no fewer than two permanent seats with the full prerogatives and privileges of permanent membership. Including the right of veto if the veto continues to exist. And no fewer than five non-permanent seats. The selection of Africa's representatives in both categories must be done by the African Union for submission to the General Assembly for election. On this, the L69 is unambiguous. On the question of veto, the L69 and the African model speak with one voice. Both hold that the veto ought to be abolished. Both hold, but with equal firmness, that so long as it exists, any new permanent members must enjoy it as a matter of elementary justice. A two-tier permanent membership in which some permanent members hold the veto and others do not would not constitute reform. It would entrench a new hierarchy dressed in the language of progress and reform. The L69 group does not accept that outcome. The L69 model proposes a total of 27 seats, with an affirmative vote of 15 required for decision. The African model proposes no fewer than 26. These positions are also aligned. Both proceed from the same logic. Expansion must be genuine. The developing world must be duly represented, and the resulting Council must be capable of acting with legitimacy and The L69 remains open to the precise configuration that best serves these shared objectives. The L69 notes with the extensive convergence between the Africa model and our own positions on working methods and the relationship between the Council and the General Assembly. Both groupings call for a more transparent, democratic and accountable Councils. Both insist on the Charter-mandated prerogatives of the General Assembly and resist the Council's encroachment on the General Assembly's authority. Both call for a more systematic, with troop-contributing countries, responsible invocation of Chapter VII and not treating sanctions as instruments of narrow political interest. There is one element of the L69 model that the Africa model does not address, and we wish to note it not as a point of divergence, but as a complementary contribution to our shared reform agenda. The L69 group advocates for a dedicated rotating non-permanent seat for small island developing states across all regions. This proposal was advanced by CARICOM, itself inspired by the foundation work of the C10, and was subsequently embraced by the L69. It reflects the particular vulnerabilities and perspectives that SIDS bring to questions of international peace and security, most acutely on climate-related security threats. This proposal is not a point of divergence with the African model. It addresses a separate and equally compelling gap in the Council's representational architecture. We note that it has attracted growing support across groupings, and we warmly invite the C-10 to consider whether the Africa model might, in future iterations, find accommodation for it. The L69 group notes with interest the Africa model's affirmation that the selection of Africa's representatives for the permanent categories shall be done by the African Union for submission to the General Assembly for election. The group fully supports this principle. It is consistent with the spirit of the common African position and with Africa's sovereign right to determine its own representation. We raise, in a spirit of cordiality and in anticipation of questions that the wider membership will eventually pose, on one matter that the CTEEN may wish to elaborate upon as the process advances. which is the modalities by which the African Union will identify the two candidates for the permanent category. The L69 group looks forward to the CTEN's further guidance on this question, which we are confident will strengthen the case for reform. In closing, the submission of the African model is a significant moment in this process. The Pact for the Future called for models. Africa has delivered one with precision and authority. The L69 stands alongside the C10 in the conviction that reform is not merely desirable, but necessary, not merely procedural, but moral. We will continue to advance this agenda together. We thank the presenter and co-chairs. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of Saint Lucia, and I give the floor to Trinidad and Tobago.

Thank you, co-chairs. I have the honor to deliver this intervention on behalf of the 14 member states of the Caribbean Community, CARICOM. I thank the distinguished delegation of Sierra Leone for the presentation of the African model for reform of the Security Council. as contained in the Izulwini Consensus on Security Declaration. CARICOM reaffirms its support for the African common position on reform of the Security Council. We reiterate that the current imbalance on the Security Council with the non-representation of both the African and Latin American and Caribbean regions in the permanent category of which the Security Council must be addressed in any reform of the said Council. We therefore continue to advocate for a reformed Council that adequately reflects the current membership of the United Nations, which necessitates expansion in both the permanent and non-permanent categories of membership. This is the only way to address the historical injustice against Africa. Distinguished Co-Chairs, Caricom has taken note of the commonalities between its own model for reform of the Council and the African model, including on the question of the veto and the categories of membership. We have also noted the divergence regarding regional representation, particularly the assertion that Africa is the only region not represented in the permanent category of the Security Council. CARICOM would welcome a further elaboration of this, given that of the five electoral regions from which members of the Security Council are drawn, both Africa and Latin America and the Caribbean are not represented in the permanent category. Importantly as well, the absence of any commentary by Africa on CARICOM's proposal for a rotating seat across all regions that contains SIDS is notable given the implications for the African group as a region as well. CARICOM would therefore welcome Africa's view on this proposal, particularly on how it sees this proposal aligning with its own advocacy for increased non-permanent seats. Distinguished Co-Chairs, I offer one concluding point, that is to express CARICOM's support for any efforts to develop a consolidated model. We believe that this is an important step towards achieving the long overdue reform that we have been seeking in this IGM since 2009. Please be assured that CARICOM will continue to be a constructive partner to this end. I thank you, Co-Chairs.
I thank the distinguished representative of Trinidad and Tobago. I give the floor to the Republic of Korea.

Distinguished Co-Chairs, we express our appreciation for the efforts undertaken by Sierra Leone to coordinate and present the African model on behalf of the African Union. The Republic of Korea aligns itself with the statement made by the Permanent Representative of Italy on behalf of the Uniting for Consensus Group. I would now like to add the following brief points in my national capacity. First, the APEC's position has long been recognized through the Declaration of 1999 and the Consensus of 2005. The Republic of Korea fully shares the view that we must redress the historical injustice against APEC as a priority. And while taking APEC as a special case, improve the representation to other underrepresented and unrepresented regions and groups, such as Asia Pacific and Latin America and Caribbean. A Security Council that appears to poorly integrate the voices and leadership of these underrepresented groups simply cannot claim to be truly representative or effective in managing the oversized peace and security challenges of our time. Second, while we continue to strive for representativeness and democracy, these must not be achieved at the expense of the Council's accountability, effectiveness and efficiency. My delegation holds the principled position that expanding the number of permanent members and extending veto power which fundamentally undermine these core values. Thus, we believe that Council reform should be focused on the expansion of the elected non-permanent category. Against this backdrop, we seek to remedy current imbalances by adhering to the principle of equitable geopolitical geographical distribution enshrined in Article 13, paragraph 1 of the Charter. We advocate for reformed Council that include long-term elected seats with the possibility of re-election to foster both inclusivity and continuity. Specifically, to treat Africa as a special case, we envision an enlargement where the African group is assigned the highest number of additional seats, totaling six non-permanent seats, to ensure its rightful and enhanced presence in Council. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative of the Republic of Korea, and I give the floor to France.

Thank you, distinguished co-chairs. Thank you for convening this debate, and I thank the PR of Sierra Leone for presenting the African model, which was long awaited. An expanded Council to allow states that have the capacity and will to do so to contribute to international peacekeeping and security. In this regard, I recall that France has clearly and constantly supported since 2005 the creation of two permanent seats for African states, as well as the candidacy of Germany, India, Japan, and Brazil to the non-permanent member seats that will be created in their geographic groups. As for veto rights, we agree with the African Group on two points. thank the representative of France for his statement and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Egypt

co-chairs I first wish to thank Ambassador Michael Imran Kanu the permanent representative of Sierra Leone coordinator of the African group of 10 for presenting the African model on the reform of the UN Security Council and for all his efforts overseeing it throughout all the stages leading up to today's discussion. No reform of the Council can claim credibility, legitimacy, or balance if it fails to correct the continued exclusion of Africa from permanent representation, despite the fact that the Council's agenda has for decades been heavily focused on African issues. Third, We underscore that the African model is not a partial or a selective proposal. It is a comprehensive and integrated framework. It addresses the categories of membership, regional representation, the question of the veto, the size of an enlarged council, the working methods of the council, and the relationship between the Security Council and the General Assembly. In this regard, Egypt emphasizes that serious engagement with the African model requires engagement with it in its entirety, not only with the selected elements of it. In line with the African model, Africa must be allocated no fewer than two permanent seats and five non-permanent seats. Egypt stresses that this is an essential component of respecting Africa's collective position and its legitimate right to determine its own representation. This selection shall be treated no differently. Fifth, Egypt further stresses the importance of the model's reaffirmation that Africa must be treated as a special case and priority in the reform process. This is fully justified by history, by present realities, and by the long-standing underrepresentation of the continent in the Council structure. Any meaningful reform must therefore place the redress of Africa's injustice at its core, not at the margins. Last but not least, on the question of the veto, Egypt reiterates the principled African position. Africa is opposed to the veto. However, so long as the veto continues to exist, it must be extended to new permanent members. Thank you, Co-Chair, distinguished Co-Chairs, dear Tarek and Lise, Ambassador Cano, dear Michael, colleagues, today marks a significant milestone in our efforts to advance Security Council reform. The presentation of the African model is not a procedural step forward.

In global governance and be equitably represented on the Security Council.

The composition of the Security Council reflects a world that is long gone. The world of 1945, where the majority of African countries were still under colonial rule. A stronger and more equitable representation for Africa on the Council is not only a matter of inclusivity or a matter of justice, it is a matter of legitimacy and effectiveness of the Council alike. Many of these avenues.

Which concrete division of new permanent seats and additional non-permanent seats the African Group envisions between the different regional groups. Would this be similar to the draft resolution A/59/67 presented by the African Group in 2005? In the IGN.

Council and both in an informal and informal settings. I thank you.

Thank you, Co-Chair. We thank you for convening this meeting of the IGM dedicated to the model discussion, one that we have been looking forward to. I thank the distinguished representative of Turkey for his statement. And I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Belgium on behalf of the Benelux countries.

Mr. Chair, Madam Chair. I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the Benelux countries, the Kingdom of the Netherlands, Luxembourg, and my own country, Belgium. Consistent with our long-standing position and in line with the commitments set out in the Pact for the Future, the Benelux countries reiterate that Security Council reform must make the Council more representative, democratic, transparent, accountable and effective, reflecting today's geopolitical realities rather than those of 1945. In this regard, we welcome several important elements of the African model. On the categories of membership, we would also be open to consider a pragmatic compromise should this proposal form a bridge between groups, provided it enhances representativeness, democratic legitimacy, accountability and effectiveness. Second, we appreciate the strong emphasis placed on improving the working methods of the Council, including greater transparency, enhanced accountability, strengthened engagement with troop and police contributing countries, and closer cooperation between the Security Council and the General Assembly. Could you elaborate on the proposed selection process by the African Union. In addition, would you consider the possibility of presenting more than one candidate per seat for election by the General Assembly? Second, on the size and composition of an enlarged Council, we note a proposal for a Council of no fewer than 26 members. In this context, we would be grateful for the African Group's view on the following question: How does the African Group envisage the allocation of additional seats both permanent and non-permanent, to other regional groups in an enlarged Council, particularly with regard to ensuring appropriate balance among regions, in line with the parameters set out in action 39 of the Pact for the Future, and the meaningful inclusion of developing countries and small and medium-sized States. The Benelux countries remain convinced that the question of the veto is central to Security Council reform. Its use has too often prevented the Council from fulfilling its primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security. We therefore believe that any reform must carefully consider ways to limit the adverse effects of the veto while preserving the Council's ability to act decisively. Mr. Chair, Madam Chair, in closing, the Benelux countries see the African model as an important and substantial contribution to this process and as a significant building block for the development towards a consolidated reform model. We stand ready to engage constructively with the African Group and all Member States with a view to achieving a reform of the Security Council that effectively redresses underrepresentation, and existing imbalances enhances legitimacy and strengthens the Council's capacity to carry out its primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace and security. I thank you.

Co-Chairs, I thank you for convening this meeting on model discussion as we strive to translate the IGM process into tangible progress. Third, we see convergences on the African model regarding the Council's working methods. Indonesia supports the efforts for a full implementation of transparency measures, such as Note 507, and improvements in the pen-holdership mechanism to ensure a more balanced role between permanent and non-permanent members. We take note with interest the African models call to enhance the Council's relationship with troop and police contributing countries, particularly during the early stages of mission planning and mandate implementation. Indonesia also continues to call for a more comprehensive and analytical annual reports by the Security Council to the General Assembly. Co-chairs, this reform process is a chance to ensure the UN remains relevant and fit for purpose. You can count on Indonesia's unwavering commitment to contribute constructively in this endeavor. Let me start by underlining that Pakistan firmly believes in the principle of sovereign equality, which must remain central in the reform debate as a guarantee for a more democratic, transparent and representative Security Council. And let me reiterate in that context that Pakistan has consistently affirmed its understanding that Africa's call, as articulated in the Asylwini Consensus and the Sirte Declaration, is not a pursuit of privilege, but a desire for justice and equity. Africa's demand for permanent seats is for the entire region. and is therefore different from other proposals, such as that of the G4, that seek permanent membership for individual states. As we understand it, against the two empowered seats which are sought by Africa, representation on the Council could be from two at a time or through rotation by a larger number of African states under arrangements to be made by Africa itself. Through this, Africa would thus retain the power to ensure accountability on the part of those states which would represent it and act on its behalf in the Council and, by extension, the wider membership. Co-Chairs, on the model presented, I would like to make the following additional points in my national capacity. One. Pakistan opposes the creation of new permanent seats as it is contrary to the universally agreed principles of democracy, accountability and transparency. Our policy is based on principles which seek to democratize the Council through reform, that promotes the interests and aspirations of all UN Member States. We believe that additional elected members will enhance regional representation and ownership, thereby imparting more legitimacy to the Council. Second, we would like to inquire about the total number of permanent seats that this model has envisaged. Are the additional four permanent seats meant for regional groups, and how have they been configured? If Africa aspires for a model based on regional representation, we understand it would have propagated the same for other seats it has proposed, and those should be subject to consensus among the respective groups. Third, we believe that injustice has also been done to other regions such as the Asia Pacific and the Latin American Caribbean regions as well as cross regional groups such as the Arab group, the SEADs and OIC. My own country and many other countries sitting here have experienced colonization and were not even members of the UN when the charter was signed. These regions should also be treated equally in terms of representation. Moreover, speaking hypothetically, according to the current assumption, if the total number of seats allotted to Africa were to be seven, then for other regions which have experienced injustice, it would be legitimate to ask for a similar proportionate increase in the number of seats, thus bringing to the fore the question about the possible size of the Council and its relative efficiency and effectiveness. Asia, for example, with almost equal number of members should also have seven seats. Fourth, we acknowledge the space provided in the model for regional representation. We would like to underline that in line with the commitment of our leaders in the Pact for the Future, there was also an acknowledgement of the need to accommodate the concerns pertaining to the representation of cross-regional groups such as the small island developing states, Arab states, and the Organization of Islamic Cooperation. And let me recall that UFC was the first group to formally propose a dedicated seat for SIDS. Co-Chairs, the UFC and African positions are compatible in many ways, most notably on regional representation, concept of rotation and consensus. The U.S. proposal has the flexibility to respond to the African desire for stronger and continuing representation on the Council based on regional consensus. Our proposal could also ensure representation of all the subregions of Africa. Similarly, Africa's demand for veto is for and on behalf of the entire African region, not for one or two states. While Pakistan's position on veto is well known, and as we said in the veto discussion on 14th April, mechanisms could be developed to provide Africa with the collective ability to protect its interests and positions as a region, even where there would be no extension of veto in a reformed Council. Most importantly, another commonality between the positions of UFC and that of the African Union is our shared desire to achieve a result based on the broadest possible agreement. African demand, as we see it, has unified the African region and has thus gained understanding and support from the rest of the membership. This support cannot be compared with the aspirants of individual permanent seats whose unilateral claims have led to serious divisions in their respective regions and the wider membership. Co-Chairs, in conclusion, rectifying the injustice suffered by Africa is not a matter of concession, but of principle. Pakistan stands ready to work constructively with Africa and all partners for a just, democratic and representative Council truly reflective of the Charter's promise and responsiveness to the realities of our times. A reform for all, a privilege for none. Thank you.

Distinguished co-chairs, excellencies, and colleagues. I thank the co-chairs for convening today's discussion that focuses on the African model of United Nations Security Council reform. India fully aligns with the statements.

Delivered by the PR of Saint Lucia on behalf of L69 and PR of Brazil on behalf of G4. In addition, I would like to deliver the following in my national capacity. At the outset, India wholeheartedly welcomes the presentation of the African model and thanks our friends from the region who.

Worked tirelessly towards its realization.

To pursue national political agendas. This is true for the sanctions as well, as alluded to in the African model.

A smooth channel of communication and enabling processes must guide these interactions.

Finally, India would like to stress that efforts aimed at achieving.

Expansion in the non-permanent category only would not result in real and substantive reform.

India's endeavor has been to reduce the existing inequities by expanding both categories of membership and thereby increase the representativeness of the Security Council and bring about greater balance between permanent and non-permanent members and change the political dynamics of the Council for better outcomes on peace and security issues.

More representativeness translates to more democracy.

In closing, I am happy to note that the African model fully encapsulates this spirit. I thank you, Co-Chairs.

Leadership as coordinator of the African Union Committee of Ten and for circulating the African model.

Which should be treated as a key element of the reform process.

Progress towards a Council that is more representative and better able to respond to the challenges that we face today.
